title: Inside a Restored 1949 Lucknow Heritage Home Where Slow Living Takes Centre Stage
excerpt: Digital creator Geetika Chakravarti's tour of her family's 1949 Lucknow residence — restored by her parents 11 years ago — is a love letter to verandahs, jali cutouts and unhurried mornings.
body:
• Digital creator Geetika Chakravarti has opened up her family's restored 1949 heritage home in Lucknow in an Instagram reel, "slow living in my 1949 home in Lucknow."
  • The house was restored by her parents nearly 11 years ago, keeping its verandahs, jali cutouts, bamboo chiks, dark wood staircases and terrazzo floors intact.
  • For travellers: Lucknow's old neighbourhoods reward the slow itinerary — heritage walks, colonial-era architecture and courtyard homes like this one are the city's real draw.
  • Chakravarti, now Mumbai-based, lived in the house full-time for six years; her family also visited her maternal grandmother's home in Allahabad yearly.

Sometimes luxury is not a penthouse but a verandah with a bamboo blind, a lawn, and time. In an Instagram reel titled "slow living in my 1949 home in Lucknow," digital creator Geetika Chakravarti takes viewers inside her family's ancestral residence — a house built in 1949, lovingly restored by her parents nearly 11 years ago, and kept deliberately, stubbornly un-modern.

What the house looks like

The tour moves through the small rituals that make the house feel lived-in rather than staged. A hand-painted botanical mural behind the bed brings tropical palms into the bedroom. The verandah — with traditional jali-style cutouts and woven bamboo blinds known as chiks — overlooks the gardens and doubles as the family's favourite spot to eat, relax and spend time with her dog. Expansive lawns surround the property; in one playful moment, Chakravarti tries mowing the grass with a traditional hand mower, captioning it "tried to mow the lawn as my workout lol."

Inside, the interiors celebrate mid-century Indian domestic architecture: dark wooden staircases, gallery walls of botanical prints, brass antiques and terrazzo flooring. Nothing is over-restored. The architectural details and vintage elements are allowed to stay central to the home's identity while it continues to serve modern life.

Context: why this resonates

Heritage homes are having a cultural moment in India — and the resonance is sharpest for the diaspora. For Indians abroad, the ancestral home is often the single most emotionally charged asset the family still holds: a place visited every few years, maintained by relatives, freighted with memory. Chakravarti's connection with the house goes back to childhood visits, and she later lived there full-time for nearly six years, though Mumbai is now her primary base. Her family also visited her maternal grandmother's home in Allahabad almost every year when they came to India — a rhythm familiar to every NRI household with roots in two cities.

"Even before moving here, we would visit this house and my nani's home in Allahabad almost every year," Chakravarti reflected. "I have a lot of fond memories attached to this house, and I feel a sense of warmth and comfort every time I visit."

The travel angle: Lucknow for the heritage traveller

Lucknow is underrated on the diaspora travel circuit, which skews toward the Golden Triangle and Goa. The city's old quarters — the Residency, the Rumi Darwaza, the chikanari workshops — reward exactly the slow itinerary Chakravarti's reel models: verandah mornings, garden afternoons, architecture as the activity. For NRIs planning a roots trip to Uttar Pradesh, the heritage-home stay category is growing: restored havelis and colonial-era bungalows converted into boutique accommodation let visitors live the aesthetic rather than just photograph it.

Practically: the best months for Lucknow are October through March; the city's old-city heritage walks are the fastest way to orient yourself; and if your family still holds an ancestral property, restoration economics have improved — craftspeople for lime plaster, terrazzo and woodwork are in demand again.

What's next

Chakravarti's reel is part of a wider creator-led reappraisal of India's domestic architecture — the homes that were never meant to be content, now finding audiences of millions. The slow-living aesthetic it sells may be curated, but the house itself is real, and that is the point.
